lines.trans: I won a lucky ticket.
When do new relationships begin?
Then a bright flame flares up.
Over time a flame can go out.
But just one spark is enough.
Are you running away again today?
No, I am not running away.
Everything is just happening so fast.

lines.trans: Do you feel bad with me right now?
I feel very good with you.

words.gloss: to me (мне некогда = I have no time)

lines.trans: Katya, I beg you, stay.
All right, I will stay a little longer.

meanings.note: Document for entry or travel. Common masculine noun meaning 'ticket' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Нина, у меня есть второй билет.
examples.trans: Nina, I have a second ticket.
Listen here, we bought tickets after all!

meanings.note: the comparative 'быстрее', often as an order
the comparative 'быстрее', often as an order

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

meanings.note: The neuter form 'всё' used alone. Core Russian det meaning 'all, whole; everyone, everything' in everyday speech.
Neuter всё. Core Russian det meaning 'all, whole; everyone, everything' in everyday speech.
Plural все. Core Russian det meaning 'all, whole; everyone, everything' in everyday speech.
Проводить время = to spend time. Common neuter noun meaning 'time' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'bright', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Then a bright flame flares up.
The match flares up and goes out right away.

meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (stem 'играть'). Used as a perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to win', paired with 'выигрывать'.

examples.text: Паша, эти выборы ты не выиграешь.
examples.trans: Pasha, you won't win this election.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: That is quite enough for you.

examples.text: Для настоящей любви этого вполне достаточно.
examples.trans: For true love this is quite enough.

meanings.note: in threats: ты ещё увидишь = you'll see
Core Russian adv meaning 'more; still; yet' in everyday speech.
Ещё больше = even more. Core Russian adv meaning 'more; still; yet' in everyday speech.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (root 'рождаться'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to new'.

examples.text: Дружба может зарождаться в самых неожиданных местах.
examples.trans: Friendship can begin in the most unexpected places.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'enough', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: But just one spark is enough.
Bright sparks flew from the campfire.

meanings.note: Question word and conjunction. Core Russian adv meaning 'when' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: When I grow up, I'll be the mayor.

meanings.note: Agreeing, often reluctantly. Core Russian part meaning 'all right, OK' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: All right, here you go. There, look.

meanings.note: Short for может быть. Core Russian part meaning 'maybe, perhaps' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: I thought maybe you wouldn't see me.

meanings.note: + infinitive. Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'can, to be able', paired with 'смочь'.

examples.text: Этого не может быть. Это наша история.
examples.trans: That can't be. It's our history.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates
Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'много'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: I need to do a bit of work.

examples.text: Мы даём вам ещё немного времени.
examples.trans: We are giving you a little more time.

meanings.note: + genitive: 'у нас нет выбора' = we have no choice
+ genitive. Core Russian part meaning 'no; there isn't' in everyday speech.
Stronger contrast than 'а'. Core Russian conj meaning 'but' in everyday speech.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.
I want to, but I can't.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('new').

examples.text: Ну что, довольна? Теперь новую работу искать.
examples.trans: Well, happy now? Now I have to look for a new job.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'one', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Нам очень дорого обходится авторская кухня.
examples.trans: Auteur cuisine costs us very dearly.

examples.text: Это все, кто выходил из отеля.
examples.trans: That is everyone who left the hotel.
What is going on here right now?

meanings.note: Often with annoyance. Core Russian adv meaning 'again' in everyday speech.

examples.text: Нина, не слушай. Это опять обман.
examples.trans: Nina, don't listen. It's another trick.

meanings.note: ничего не осталось = there's nothing left

Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as a perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to remain, to be left', paired with 'оставаться'.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: Between people or groups. Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'attitude, relation; (pl.) relationship' in everyday Russian.
Towards someone or something. Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'attitude, relation; (pl.) relationship' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: А я испорчу отношения с будущим мэром.
examples.trans: And I'll ruin my relationship with the future mayor.
We have a very warm relationship.

examples.text: Ты с ума сошёл? У нас с тобой только деловые отношения!
examples.trans: Have you lost your mind? Between you and me it's strictly business!

meanings.note: With verbs: очень люблю. Core Russian adv meaning 'very, very much' in everyday speech.
With verbs: очень люблю. Core Russian adv meaning 'very, very much' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'flares', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Then a bright flame flares up.
Over time a flame can go out.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.
Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Послушайте, а можно в другое место? Здесь плохо пахнет.
examples.trans: Listen, could we go somewhere else? It smells bad in here.

побыть.gloss: to stay for a while, to be (briefly)

meanings.en: to be, to spend a little time
meanings.note: побыть одной / одному = to be alone for a while

examples.trans: Let's stay here a little longer.

examples.text: Забирайте и уходите. Я хочу побыть одна.
examples.trans: Take it and go. I want to be alone.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (root 'тухнуть'). Used in Russian as a perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to out'.

examples.trans: Over time a flame can go out.

examples.text: Костёр может потухнуть, если не подкладывать дрова.
examples.trans: The campfire may go out if you do not add wood.

meanings.en: to happen, take place, go on
meanings.note: Что происходит? = What is going on?

examples.trans: What is going on? I don't understand.

examples.text: Мы не знаем, что с нашей дочерью происходит!
examples.trans: We don't know what is happening with our daughter!

meanings.note: просить прощения = to ask for forgiveness
Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to ask (for)', paired with 'попросить'.

examples.text: Когда вырасту, ты будешь просить у меня прощения!
examples.trans: When I grow up, you'll be begging me to forgive you!

meanings.note: 'это просто' = it's easy. Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.
Это просто = it's easy. Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: + instrumental; со before some consonant clusters: со всеми

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: The г sounds like в.

examples.text: Виктор Степанович, сегодня никак не могу.
examples.trans: Viktor Stepanovich, I really can't today.

meanings.note: 'сейчас буду' = I'll be right there

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Сч is pronounced like щ. Qualitative adjective formed with the productive suffix '-тельный'/'-ливый'. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('happy; lucky').
Qualitative adjective formed with the productive suffix '-тельный'/'-ливый'. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('happy; lucky').
Счастливый конец = happy ending. Qualitative adjective formed with the productive suffix '-тельный'/'-ливый'. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('happy; lucky').

examples.trans: The film has a happy ending.

examples.text: Ты сейчас один против всех. Счастливого конца не будет.
examples.trans: Right now you're alone against everyone. There won't be a happy ending.

meanings.note: At the start of a question. Core Russian part meaning 'so, then; like that' in everyday speech.
Core Russian part meaning 'so, then; like that' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: At that time. Core Russian adv meaning 'then, back then' in everyday speech.
Core Russian adv meaning 'then, back then' in everyday speech.

examples.text: Я тебе тогда сказал: ты меня ещё поцелуешь.
examples.trans: I told you back then: you'll kiss me one day.

meanings.note: softens a request: только не сердись = just don't be angry
One person, informal. Core Russian pron meaning 'you (informal)' in everyday speech.

meanings.note: Case forms. Core Russian pron meaning 'you (informal)' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Intransitive verb. Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'бегать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to run away, escape', paired with 'убежать'.

examples.trans: I am not going to run away.
The dog is running away into the park.
I am not planning to run away anywhere.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('good, nice').

examples.text: Какое хорошее утро! Лидия Алексеевна, чашку кофе, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: What a lovely morning! Lidia Alekseyevna, a cup of coffee, please.

meanings.note: How something is done. Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.
As an answer. Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.
меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)

meanings.en: other forms: меня (gen/acc), мне (dat), мной (instr), мне (prep)
meanings.note: Case forms. Core Russian pron meaning 'I' in everyday speech.
Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'bright', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('vivid') (intense in flavor or color) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я просто хотел добавить яркий аромат.
examples.trans: I simply wanted to add a vivid aroma.

examples.text: Что это за странная яркая бумага?
examples.trans: What is this strange bright paper?

examples.text: Дмитрий, почему здесь выключили яркий свет?
examples.trans: Dmitry, why did they turn off the bright light here?
